Eighty-seven years ago, our founders established a new nation on this continent, built on the idea of liberty and committed to the belief that everyone is created equal.

Now we find ourselves in the midst of a great civil war, which will determine whether that nation—or any nation founded on those same ideas—can survive. We have gathered on a major battlefield from that war, and we've come here to dedicate part of this field as a burial ground for those who died so that the nation could live. This is a fitting and appropriate thing to do.

But in truth, we don't have the power to dedicate, consecrate, or hallow this ground. The brave men who fought here, both those still living and those who died, have already made this ground sacred through their actions—far more than anything we could say or do. The world won't pay much attention to what we say here today, and it won't remember our words for long, but it will never forget what these men accomplished here. Instead, it's up to us, the living, to devote ourselves to finishing the work that those who fought here have carried forward so admirably. We must dedicate ourselves to the great task still ahead of us: drawing greater commitment from the example of these honored dead to the cause they gave everything for; resolving firmly that their deaths will not be meaningless; ensuring that this nation, with God's blessing, experiences a new birth of freedom; and making certain that a government of the people, by the people, and for the people does not disappear from this earth.
